title: Foundations of Nursing Practice: Documentation & Handover
html:
Documentation and handover make nursing care visible, continuous, and safer. A clear record shows what the RN assessed, what was done, how the client responded, who was notified, and what follow-up is needed. It is not a memory aid written later or a place for vague opinions. Follow the organization’s record system, policy, approved abbreviations, and privacy requirements.

Learning goals

  • Document assessments, interventions, and responses with objective, timely language.
  • Distinguish an observable fact from an interpretation or conclusion.
  • Use SBAR to organize urgent communication and requests.
  • Give a concise handover that supports continuity and client safety.
  • Use read-back or check-back to confirm critical communication as required.

Chart what happened, when it happened, and the response

Record relevant assessment data, interventions, client teaching, communication, and outcomes as close to the event as possible. Use objective details: “respiratory rate 28; speaking in short phrases; provider notified at 1415” is clearer than “client is doing poorly.” Quote the client when their exact words explain a symptom, concern, preference, or refusal. Distinguish the client’s report from the RN’s observation and from the actions taken.

Objective does not mean incomplete
Include relevant changes, escalation, the response received, and follow-up assessment. Never chart care before it occurs, guess a time, change another person's entry, or copy a previous note without verifying that it is still accurate.

Protect privacy and the integrity of the record

Access only the record needed for your work, use approved devices and accounts, keep screens and printed information secure, and share client information only with authorized people for a care purpose. Use the approved correction process if an entry is inaccurate; do not erase or conceal the original record. Avoid unsupported blame, judgmental labels, sarcasm, or diagnoses outside nursing scope. Documentation should be professional, factual, and respectful even when the situation is difficult.

Use SBAR to communicate a concern

SBAR organizes a concise clinical conversation: Situation states who you are, which client is involved, and the immediate concern. Background gives relevant history, baseline, recent events, and treatments. Assessment shares the focused findings and what you are concerned about. Recommendation or Request states what is needed and how urgently. A request can be as direct as “Please evaluate the client now” or “Would you like an order for a bladder scan?”

When receiving a new or critical instruction, use the organization’s read-back or check-back process. Repeat the information back accurately, clarify ambiguity, document the required elements, and complete the follow-up. Do not infer an order, silently accept an unclear instruction, or delay calling because the message feels inconvenient.

Give a handover that supports continuity

A handover transfers responsibility and accountability as well as information. Include the client’s identifiers as required, code status and precautions, current condition and trend, relevant history, allergies, recent changes, assessments, ordered therapies and equipment, lines or tubes, pending tests, tasks due, safety concerns, goals, and what the next nurse should watch or do. At the bedside, protect privacy and invite the client to correct relevant information when appropriate.

Prioritize what has changed and what could cause harm on the next shift. A complete handover is not every chart detail; it is the accurate information the next clinician needs to safely continue care. If a receiver has a question, pause, clarify, and verify understanding.

Evaluate communication

After documenting or handing over, check whether the needed action occurred, whether the client was reassessed, and whether new orders or escalation steps were understood and completed. The communication loop closes only when information is received, understood, acted on, and evaluated. Update the record according to policy as the situation changes.

Clinical example

An RN observes new confusion, a temperature change, and lower blood pressure than the client's earlier baseline. The RN documents objective findings and time, uses SBAR to contact the appropriate clinician, reads back the new orders as required, completes the urgent interventions, reassesses the client, and records the response. Saying only “provider aware” would omit the critical information that supports continuity.
